summary: Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) block cipher mode built on the Encrypt-then-MAC principle, defined for 64-bit and 128-bit block ciphers. It was standardized in Russia and is used with the GOST ciphers in protocols such as TLS 1.3 and IPsec. This informational document is a reference to enable review.

plainLanguage.summary:
MGM is a way of scrambling a message and proving it was not altered, using a block cipher such as the Russian GOST ciphers.

It scrambles the data like a stream cipher and adds a short tag that the receiver checks. Anyone who changes the data, the tag or the extra context breaks the check.

subtitle: An authenticated encryption mode that works with the GOST block ciphers and with any other block cipher.

tldr.problem: Secure communication needs two things at once: the data must be unreadable to anyone else, and the receiver must be able to tell that nobody tampered with it. Doing both well needs a way of combining a block cipher with a message authentication code.
tldr.mechanism: MGM encrypts the data in counter mode, like a stream cipher, and computes an authentication tag with a multilinear function over the Galois field. The tag covers the ciphertext, the associated data and the lengths of both.
tldr.outcome: The mode was standardised in Russia and is used with the GOST ciphers in protocols such as TLS 1.3 and IPsec. This RFC is a reference so that the mechanism can be reviewed; it does not claim IETF consensus.

today: RFC 9058 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The RFC states that it does not have IETF consensus and does not imply IETF support for MGM. It exists as a reference so that the mechanisms already in use can be reviewed, and so that MGM can be used with any block cipher.

sections.title: What MGM Is For
sections.content:
Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) is a block cipher mode that provides authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD), built on the Encrypt-then-MAC principle: the data is encrypted first, and the authentication tag is then computed over the ciphertext. It is defined for use with 64-bit and 128-bit block ciphers, and the design principles can be applied to other block sizes.

MGM was standardised in Russia. It is used as an AEAD mode with the GOST block ciphers in a number of protocols, among them TLS 1.3 and IPsec. This document is a reference, so that the mechanisms in use can be reviewed and so that MGM can be used with any block cipher.

The RFC is explicit about its standing: it does not have IETF consensus and does not imply IETF support for MGM.
sections.plainLanguage:
MGM does two jobs in one. It hides the content of a message and it produces a short tag that lets the receiver prove the message was not changed on the way.

The RFC writes the method down so that cryptographers can check it and so that other block ciphers can use it.

sections.title: The Notation Used
sections.content:
The specification is written in a compact notation, and the RFC defines it precisely. V* is the set of all bit strings of any finite length, including the empty one, and substrings are counted from the right starting at zero. V_s is the set of all bit strings of length s. |X| is the length of a string in bits, and X || Y is the two strings joined end to end. a^s is the string of s copies of the bit a, and (xor) is exclusive-or of two strings of the same length.

Three conversions move between bit strings and numbers. MSB_i takes the i most significant bits of a string. Int_s reads a string as a binary number, and Vec_s is its inverse, writing a number as a bit string.

E_K is the block cipher permutation under the key K. The letter k is the length of that key in bits and n is the block size in bits. len maps a string whose length is at most 2^(n/2) - 1 to the n/2-bit representation of that length, and [+] is addition modulo 2^(n/2).

Two operations do the real work. (x) is multiplication of two polynomials over the Galois field GF(2^n): a bit string is read as a polynomial with those bits as coefficients, the two polynomials are multiplied, and the result is read back as a bit string. The field is fixed by a polynomial, which is w^64 + w^4 + w^3 + w + 1 when n is 64 and w^128 + w^7 + w^2 + w + 1 when n is 128.

The last two are counters. incr_l splits a block into a left half and a right half and adds one to the left half, keeping the right half. incr_r does the opposite and increments the right half. Both are additions in Z_(2^(n/2)).
sections.plainLanguage: The specification uses symbols rather than words, so it is worth stating what the main ones mean. The important one is the multiplication: two blocks are treated as polynomials over a finite field and multiplied, which is the step that lets the authentication tag detect any change to the data.

sections.title: Encrypting and Producing the Tag
sections.content:
One more parameter completes the definition: the bit length S of the authentication tag, where 32 <= S <= n. The value must be fixed for a given protocol, and choosing it trades message expansion against the probability of a successful forgery.

The encryption procedure takes four inputs: the encryption key K; an initial counter nonce (ICN) in V_(n-1); the associated authenticated data A, whose length is less than 2^(n/2) and which is authenticated but not encrypted; and the plaintext P, whose length is likewise less than 2^(n/2). Both A and P are split into blocks of n bits, with a possibly shorter last block. If A is empty then h is 0 and t is n; if P is empty then q is 0 and u is n.

The output is the ICN, the associated data, the ciphertext C and the authentication tag T of length S.

The procedure itself has four steps. The encryption step builds a counter block from the nonce, encrypts it to get Y_1, and increments the right half for each further block. Each full block of plaintext is exclusive-ored with the encryption of its counter block, and the last, possibly short, block uses only the leading bits of that encryption. The padding step pads the last block of associated data and the last block of ciphertext with zeroes to full blocks. The tag generation step runs a second counter, this time starting from a block built from the nonce and encrypting it to get Z_1. It multiplies each associated data block by the encryption of its counter value, exclusive-ors the results together, then does the same with the ciphertext blocks. Finally it multiplies one more counter value by the concatenation of the lengths of the associated data and the ciphertext, adds that to the running sum, encrypts the sum and takes the leading S bits as the tag. The procedure returns (ICN, A, C, T).

Two rules govern the inputs. The ICN must be chosen uniquely for every message encrypted under the same key. And the lengths of the associated data and the plaintext must satisfy 0 < |A| + |P| < 2^(n/2), so the two together are never empty and never exceed the limit.
sections.plainLanguage:
Encryption works like a stream cipher: a counter is encrypted under the key and the result is combined with the data. The tag is built from a second counter and a multiplication over the finite field, so any change to the data changes the tag.

The nonce must never repeat under the same key, and the data cannot be completely empty.

sections.title: Decrypting and Checking the Tag
sections.content:
The decryption procedure takes the key, the ICN, the associated data, the ciphertext and the received tag. It outputs either FAIL, or the associated data and the recovered plaintext.

It has four steps, and the order matters. The padding step comes first, padding the last block of associated data and the last block of ciphertext to full blocks, exactly as the sender did. The tag verification step then recomputes the tag in the same way the sender did, using the ciphertext rather than the plaintext. If the recomputed tag differs from the received one, the procedure returns FAIL and the plaintext is never produced. Only after that check passes does the decryption step run, which repeats the counter-mode encryption of the sender and exclusive-ors it with the ciphertext to recover the plaintext.

This order is the Encrypt-then-MAC principle in practice. The tag is checked over the ciphertext, so nothing is decrypted until the data has been shown to be untampered with. The length rule is the same as on the sending side: 0 < |A| + |C| < 2^(n/2).
sections.plainLanguage:
The receiver works backwards, but it checks the tag before it decrypts anything. If the tag does not match, the message is rejected and no plain text is produced.

That order is the whole point of the design: bad data never reaches the application.

sections.title: Why the Mode Is Shaped This Way
sections.content:
MGM was first proposed in a 2017 conference paper. Its design is driven by four operational properties.

It is parallelizable. Its structure is that of a counter, so the blocks E_K(Y_i) and the authentication blocks H_i are produced in counter mode, and the multilinear function itself can be evaluated in parallel.

It is inverse free. The sender never has to invert the block cipher, again because of the counter structure.

It is online, which means a message can be processed before its length is known. This works because the encryption blocks and the authentication blocks are derived from two independent source blocks, Y_i and Z_i.

It offers the availability of precomputations, meaning the values H_i and E_K(Y_i) can be calculated before any data arrives, again because the counters make them independent of the data.
sections.plainLanguage: Four practical goals shape the design. The work can be spread over several processors, the sender never has to run the cipher backwards, a message can be processed while it is still arriving, and the values can be worked out before the data turns up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists four properties that the security of MGM rests on.

The functions incr_r and incr_l are chosen so that the counter values Y_i and Z_i overlap as little as possible. The output of the multilinear function is encrypted, which resists attacks based on padding and on linear properties. The multilinear function itself is used for authentication, which resists the small subgroup attacks described in the literature. And the nonces (0^1 || ICN) and (1^1 || ICN) are encrypted, which minimises the number of plaintext and ciphertext pairs an adversary can obtain and so blocks attacks that need a lot of such material, including linear cryptanalysis, differential cryptanalysis and side-channel attacks.

Two rules are called crucial. The ICN values must be unique; using the same ICN for two different messages under the same key removes the security properties of the mode entirely. And empty plaintext and empty associated data must not be processed together, because the tag would then be independent of the nonce value, which opens the way to forgery attacks.

A security analysis exists for MGM when the block cipher is treated as a random permutation, and it gives bounds for the confidentiality advantage and the integrity advantage. For an adversary making at most q encryption queries over at most s blocks of plaintext and associated data, and allowed to produce a forgery over at most l blocks, the bounds are CA <= (3(s + 4q)^2) / 2^n and IA <= (3(s + 4q + l + 3)^2) / 2^n + 2/2^S, where n is the block size and S the tag size. The RFC says these bounds can be used as guidelines for calculating confidentiality and integrity limits.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two mistakes break the scheme: reusing a nonce under the same key, and encrypting nothing at all with no extra context. Both are called out as crucial.

The RFC also gives the published bounds on how much an attacker can learn or forge, so that a protocol can pick a tag length and usage limits that match.

items.title: Parallelizable
items.text: Encryption and authentication blocks are produced in counter mode, and the multilinear function can be evaluated in parallel.

items.title: Inverse free
items.text: The sender never has to invert the block cipher.

items.title: Online
items.text: A message can be processed before its length is known, using two independent counter blocks.

items.title: Precomputable
items.text: The values can be calculated before any data arrives.

viz.caption: THE MGM ENCRYPTION AND TAG GENERATION PROCEDURE (RFC 9058)

data.title: MGM-Encrypt(K, ICN, A, P)
data.code:
1. Encryption step:
   - if |P| = 0 then
         - C*_q = P*_q
         - C = P
   - else
     - Y_1 = E_K(0^1 || ICN),
     - For i = 2, 3, ... , q do
           Y_i = incr_r(Y_{i-1}),
     - For i = 1, 2, ... , q - 1 do
           C_i = P_i (xor) E_K(Y_i),
     - C*_q = P*_q (xor) MSB_u(E_K(Y_q)),
     - C = C_1 || ... || C*_q.

2. Padding step:
   - A_h = A*_h || 0^{n-t},
   - C_q = C*_q || 0^{n-u}.

3. Authentication tag T generation step:
   - Z_1 = E_K(1^1 || ICN),
   - sum = 0^n,
   - For i = 1, 2, ..., h do
           H_i = E_K(Z_i),
           sum = sum (xor) ( H_i (x) A_i ),
           Z_{i+1} = incr_l(Z_i),
   - For j = 1, 2, ..., q do
           H_{h+j} = E_K(Z_{h+j}),
           sum = sum (xor) ( H_{h+j} (x) C_j ),
           Z_{h+j+1} = incr_l(Z_{h+j}),
   - H_{h+q+1} = E_K(Z_{h+q+1}),
   - T = MSB_S(E_K(sum (xor) ( H_{h+q+1} (x)
                    ( len(A) || len(C) ) ))).

4. Return (ICN, A, C, T).
